title: Epigenetic drivers of cancer progression
text:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an overall mortality of 95%, even for early-stage disease, in
part because, in addition to mutations in the cancer genome, the tumors have an altered epigenome, including
chemical changes such as methylation of the DNA component cytosine, and chromatin. We will determine how
the epigenome changes from normal to pre-malignant PanIN, to cancer, to metastasis, using well-defined
genetically engineered mouse models, and we will determine the role the extracellular environment of the
cancer shapes the epigenome and is shaped by it. We will validate this work using human PDAC tissues and
cutting-edge methods for visualization of epigenetic marks in tissues, enhancing the value of the project for
eventual translation to cancer diagnosis and therapy.

title: Ultrashort Echo Time Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Knee Joint
text:
8. Project Narrative
This proposal aims to optimize and validate UTE-Adiabatic-T1 and UTE-MT-MMF techniques on knee
specimens for early OA using histopathology, biochemistry, and biomechanics as reference standards (Aim 1),
develop a multi-tissue segmentation with multi-parameter quantification net (MSMQ-Net) for simultaneous
segmentation and multi-parameter mapping of all major knee joint tissues (Aim 2), and evaluate knee changes
before and post (6, 12, and 24 months) meniscectomy for proof of principle (Aim 3). The goal is to deliver a
validated postprocessing pipeline from image acquisition to automated segmentation and UTE mapping of all
major knee tissues for early OA.

title: Identifying deficient memory replay as a potentially treatable mechanism of impaired sleep-dependent memory consolidation in schizophrenia
text:
Cognitive deficits are a core, disabling feature of schizophrenia and effective treatments are lacking.
Converging evidence from animal and human studies suggests that dysfunctional communication between the
hippocampus, a deep brain structure, and the cortex during sleep leads to memory impairment. The primary
objectives of the proposed research are to develop a sensitive physiological biomarker of hippocampal-
dependent memory consolidation, demonstrate that it is impaired in schizophrenia, and evaluate a
noninvasive, scalable technique -- closed-loop auditory stimulation during sleep -- as a potential treatment for
impaired memory in schizophrenia.

title: Epigenetic mechanisms of intestinal stem cell fate conversion in response to severe radiation injury
text:
Medical countermeasures do not exist to mitigate high-dose radiation-induced damage to the gastrointestinal
tract, so gastrointestinal acute radiation syndrome (GI-ARS) provokes high mortality after radiological
accidents. This project proposes a series of experiments to understand the specific cell populations
responsible for repopulating the intestine, using a model system mimicking GI-ARS. Successful completion of
the proposed aims will provide a foundation for future development of rational strategies to mitigate GI-ARS in
the event of radiological accidents/disasters or other settings of abdominal radiation exposure.

title: Defining Centriolar Plaque Architecture and Function Across Eukaryotic Diversity Using Expansion Microscopy and Proteomics
text:
This project investigates the structural and molecular architecture of the centriolar plaque, an atypical
microtubule-organizing center in an alveolate protist, a highly diverse eukaryotic clade comprising three major
lineages: ciliates, dinoflagellates, and apicomplexans. Employing expansion microscopy and targeted
functional analyses, we will define the roles of key CP proteins in MTOC dynamics, cell polarity, and organelle
segregation during closed mitosis. By combining high-resolution imaging with inducible knockdown systems,
this research will elucidate fundamental processes of non-canonical cell division, providing insights into the
conserved and unique strategies employed by eukaryotic cells.

title: Ecology and genetics of insecticide resistance in African malaria vectors
text:
Malaria kills more than 400 million people in Africa each year, with the majority of
fatalities occurring in children under the age of 5 in areas south of the Sahara. Control efforts have been
scaled up in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa. However, these efforts are being hampered by resistance to
commonly used insecticide for vector control. Results of these studies will help manage insecticide resistance
and malaria control.

title: In vivo targeted delivery of nucleic acids to hematopoietic stem cells for treating primary immunodeficiencies
text:
To address the limitations of current ex vivo gene and cell therapies, Optimeos Life Sciences proposes,
in this Phase I SBIR, the development of targeted nanoparticles for in vivo hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy.
This non-viral, redosable therapy aims to provide an off-the-shelf, safe, and transformative treatment for primary
immunodeficiencies.

title: Editing AMD Risk Alleles in Human Cells
text:
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of visual disability. There are two major genetic
risk factors that greatly influence one's chances of developing AMD. In this proposal, we will use novel
methods developed by members of our team for converting (“editing”) high-risk genetic variants to their
low-risk forms in human ocular cells and tissues (where the genes exert their effects) to address the
potential of gene editing for preventing the onset or delaying the progression of AMD.

title: Transcriptomic Changes during early endometriotic lesion development
text:
Despite affecting over 190 million women worldwide and being recognized for over a century, our understanding
of endometriosis pathogenesis remains limited. The proposed research will leverage cutting-edge transcriptomic
approaches to identify cellular signaling and molecular mechanisms in early lesions. By integrating molecular
data from baboon and human peritoneal lesions and applying advanced computational analyses, we will uncover
key inflammatory pathways, leading to novel therapeutic targets and advancing precision medicine for superficial
peritoneal endometriosis.

title: Sequencing and Genomics
text: SEQUENCING AND GENOMICS SHARED RESOURCE Sequencing and Genomics (SEQ) provides an integrated platform of technology, expertise, education, and infrastructure to create an accessible environment for LCCC researchers to undertake cutting-edge genomics projects. The Core specializes in six major technologies: Next Generation short-read sequencing (Illumina), long-read sequencing and genomic mapping (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, BioNano Inc.), NanoString digital RNA quantification, Affymetrix microarrays, Illumina bead array genotyping, and RNAi screening for functional validation. Through reciprocity with North Carolina State University, the SR also has access to the Pacific Biosciences Sequel system. These are complemented by LCCC investments in computational infrastructure and analysis. Over the past five years, LCCC has integrated two new units in partnership with TPF and CPDM to compliment SEQ, specifically to facilitate translational cancer genomics to seamlessly support the coordination, project management, and tracking necessary to perform genomics studies on patient samples from protocol-driven trials. In addition the Translational Genomics Laboratory (TGL) focuses solely on cancer sample preparation for downstream sequencing, NanoString analysis, or other molecular testing. This laboratory uses automated instrumentation and stable protocols optimized for limited input and degraded cancer specimens collected from clinical trials and translational studies. TGL initiates a pathway for clinical genomics projects through SEQ and subsequent analysis by the bioinformatics SR (BIOIN). SEQ SR requests $195,591, 3% of the total fiscal year 2019 budget. LCCC faculty were 43% of fiscal year 2020 users. During the past five years SEQ supported the LCCC investigators involved in TCGA. This project oversaw the molecular characterization of over 20,000 primary tumor and matched normal samples across 33 cancer types. Within the next year, SEQ will acquire an ONT PromethION 24 system, which uses a high- capacity, long-read sequencing technology capable of high production whole genome sequencing and transcriptomics. This technology allows for efficient resequencing of whole genomes including repetitive elements, structural variation, and other problematic regions of the genome. ONT sequencing provides reproducible detection of small, medium, and large size structural variations, and in the near future the detection of 5mC.

title: MSCS ENGINEERED TO PRODUCE BDNF AND GENE EDITING CARGO FOR THE TREATMENT OF HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE
text:
In accordance with the mission of the National Institute for Neurological Disorders and Stroke
(NINDS) this grant will seek fundamental knowledge about the brain and nervous system and
will use that knowledge to reduce the burden of neurological disease, specifically the feasibility
of a novel delivery platform for epigenetic DNA-binding domains such as CRISPR/Cas9. This
research holds great relevance for the advancement of treatment for those suffering from
genetically-linked neurological disorders. The funds used for this research award will be used to
develop a research pathway to critically evaluate an engineered stem cell delivery platform in a
translationally relevant animal model to facilitate this approach towards clinical trials.

title: Cellular Molecular Biology Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – CELLULAR AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY CORE The Cellular and Molecular Biology Core (CMBC) was established in 2006 to primarily assist NORC members in the assessment of adipose tissue morphology and function. Since then, the Core has consistently broadened and updated its scope and scientific focus to meet the changing needs of the NORC Research Base and incorporate key scientific advances. The CMBC assists NORC investigators conducting leading-edge research into the cellular and molecular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of obesity-associated complications and the contribution of disruptive alterations in nutrient intake/metabolism. The CMBC provides critical infrastructure, technical support, and consultation and training for mechanistic studies of adipose tissue, muscle, liver, and endothelium. Support for assessment of intercellular crosstalk through extracellular vesicles (EVs), an emerging research area, has been developed and added to the Core during the current funding cycle. The CMBC enhances and facilitates sophisticated research in nutrition and obesity by providing the following services: 1) Cellular and molecular assessments needed for mechanistic studies: i) adipose tissue characterization, ii) optimized protocols for study of cellular and tissue metabolism, iii) cell lines (mouse and human pre- adipocytes, adipocytes, myoblasts, macrophages, endothelial cells) with optimized culture and differentiation protocols, iv) isolation of preadipocytes, immune cells and endothelial cells from the stromal vascular fraction of mouse and human adipose tissue, v) multiplex assays of adipokine, myokine, hepatokine, and cytokine concentrations in plasma or cell culture media, and vi) isolation, characterization, and study of EVs (small EVs or exosomes, and microvesicles). In the next cycle, the CMBC will develop and offer new services for vii) determination of EV cell type of origin and content, viii) 3-dimensional co-culture systems and tissue on a chip cultures, and ix) access to metabolomic, lipidomic, and proteomic analyses of cells, media, and EVs. 2) Access to specialized equipment needed for metabolic investigation. During the current cycle, equipment upgrades have been completed and a new cutting-edge high sensitivity Cytek flow cytometer has been incorporated into the Core. 3) Expert consulting services in integrative cellular and molecular physiology to allow investigators at any level of experience to conduct mechanistic research in nutrition/obesity. During the current cycle, consultation on EV isolation and services for detailed EV characterization have been added. Most CMBC services are not available in other cores and are completely unique at Washington University, providing critical and cost-effective research support for NORC investigators. In addition, the CMBC interacts closely with both the NORC Clinical Sciences Research Core (CSRC) and the Animal Model Research Core (AMRC) to analyze samples from research participants and animals, providing a comprehensive, integrated interpretation of study outcomes.

title: Engineering virus-like particles for systemic and targeted RNA delivery to the brain
text:
We aim to revolutionize RNA therapeutics by engineering virus-like particles (VLPs) that can efficiently deliver
RNA to the brain across the blood-brain barrier, overcoming the limitations of current delivery systems like lipid
nanoparticles. Our approach builds on our previous successes on AAV vector engineering technology and fo-
cuses on developing VLPs targeting specific BBB receptors and establishing scalable screening platforms for
their systematic optimization. This innovative toolkit will not only transform efficient brain-targeted RNA delivery
but also establish technologies applicable to diverse therapeutic targets, ultimately bringing hope to millions
suffering from CNS disorders who currently lack effective treatments.

title: In Vivo Base Editing via Lipid Nanoparticles Targeting the Trabecular Meshwork for Glaucoma Therapy
text:
Narratives
Primary open-angle glaucoma is a major cause of irreversible blindness, and current treatments
fail to address the root molecular pathology in the trabecular meshwork. This project will develop
a one-time, non-viral gene editing therapy targeting MYOC, the most common genetic cause of
glaucoma, with the potential to restore outflow function and prevent vision loss permanently.
Results will advance a safer and more precise genome editing platform toward clinical translation.

title: Itaconate as an antimicrobial metabolite against Listeria monocytogenes infection
text:
Macrophages are highly plastic innate immune cells that coordinate host defense, tissue repair, and
homeostasis, and their dysregulation contributes to infection, chronic inflammation, metabolic disease, and
cancer. My research investigates how metabolite signaling—particularly itaconate-mediated alkylation of the
lysosomal reductase GILT—regulates macrophage antimicrobial defense. By defining these molecular
mechanisms, I aim to uncover strategies to reprogram macrophage activity and develop new therapeutic
approaches for infection and inflammatory disease.

title: Pacific Northwest Undiagnosed Disease Network Clinical Site
text: The application of genomics and other specialized evaluation to diagnosis rare human disorders, has been centered in major medical centers. The Undiagnosed Disease Network (UDN) extends the reach of rare disease evaluation and diagnosis by providing access to the undiagnosed patient in all communities. We propose an additional four years of funding for the Pacific Northwest Undiagnosed Diseases Network Clinic (PNW UDN) site to further the goals of the UDN and to provide UDN access for under- or non-insured participants in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Developing DNA-Based Molecular Robots
text:
The proposed project is relevant to public health because it will result in a series of preliminary data that will
inform future grant applications that aim to develop inexpensive and fast molecular robots to diagnose and
treat diseases. The proposed robot will detect breast cancer microRNAs and regulate the expression of
select genes that serve as therapeutic agents. If successful, the robot enables more convenient means of
theranostics, and since RNA molecules are linked to many diseases, the robot has a broader reach than
cancer medicine.

title: Human papillomavirus entry: late trafficking and establishment of infection
text:
Human Papillomaviruses infect keratinocytes in the skin and mucosa and induce epithelial tumors. In order to
cause disease virus has to deliver its genome to the nucleus of the basal cells of this stratified epithelia. Herein,
we propose to fill gaps in our understanding of late events of viral trafficking and establishment of infection, which
in turn allows identification of novel targets for prevention.

title: Biologically Plausible Computational Models of Perirhinal Cortex
text:
Human behaviors seamlessly integrate perceptual and mnemonic information. To understand how the brain
supports these abilities, this project will develop and evaluate biologically plausible computational models of
medial temporal lobe-dependent behaviors, incorporating traditional neuroscientific methods within a deep
learning framework. This integrated approach provides an unprecedented opportunity for understanding both
typical and atypical memory-related behaviors, laying a foundation for future work to develop diagnostic and
therapeutic tools to treat mnemonic-related disorders.

title: Defining broadly neutralizing antibody pharmacokinetics-pharmacodynamics in curative HIV trials
text:
This study aims to establish how differing exposure of combinations of anti-HIV targeted antibodies (bnAbs)
work to induce post treatment viral control when antiretroviral therapy (ART) is stopped (i.e., analytic treatment
interruption, ATI). Nearly a dozen completed studies of dual bnAbs have shown highly variable impact on a
person’s ability to suppress HIV following bnAb and ART washout with no clear understanding of drivers of
treatment response. Here we propose foundational studies of bnAb pharmacology, including an analysis of
bnAb-virus interactions, distribution of bnAbs to tissue using whole body imaging, and mathematical modeling
to determine how trial design and bnAb kinetics may result in post-intervention control.
